A working library · Luca

Read the sources. Mark what is still argued.

Five wings of one method. Every claim here carries where it came from and where specialists disagree — because the disagreement is usually the part worth having.

Colophon

This is a library, not a credential. It holds what I have read, what I think it means, and — deliberately, in every wing — the places where the people who know most still disagree. A claim without its dispute is half a claim.

The five wings are one method applied to five kinds of material. The Press is ideas; Lives is people worth a whole book; The Atlas is the sources I actually listen to and the principles more than one of them arrived at independently; The Field Manuals are what I hold, written as positions rather than advice; The Slipway is the trade book — the operating lessons of people who build things, kept the way sailors kept a chandlery: everything you need before setting out, each item marked with where it came from.

Set in EB Garamond and IBM Plex Mono. Assembled by hand and with AI assistance; figures are checked against a named source, and where I have corrected myself the correction stays visible rather than being quietly patched. The reading wings are set on paper. The Atlas is the only room kept dark, because a star chart is the one thing that genuinely needs a night sky.

The portraits in Lives are public-domain engravings, paintings and photographs, reduced to the house duotone and set as plates. A life without a safely public image carries the press mark instead of a borrowed picture, which seems the more honest trade. One life is in that position today: Henrietta Lacks, whose entry says why at length, and whose estate has itself disputed the use of family photographs. Two plates are licensed rather than public domain, and are credited here because the licence requires it: the Mandela photograph is by South Africa The Good News (sagoodnews.co.za) under CC BY 2.0, and the Steve Jobs photograph was taken at WWDC in 2010 by Matthew Yohe under CC BY-SA 3.0. One more is neither: the 1939 photograph of Robert Moses is by C. M. Stieglitz for the New York World-Telegram & Sun, held by the Library of Congress, which states that it knows of no copyright restrictions on it — a narrower claim than public domain, and worth saying in those words. Everything else came through Wikimedia Commons.

Disclosure

This site was assembled by Luca with substantial help from an AI assistant (Anthropic's Claude) — drafting, checking figures against the named sources, and the build itself. The picks, positions and errors are mine; when an error is found it joins the corrections above instead of disappearing. Lines marked “after” a name are compressed notes of someone's idea, not their words, and nobody named on this site has endorsed it or its readings of them. Portraits are public-domain images, except one CC BY credit noted above. The page sets no cookies and runs no analytics; the night-reading switch is remembered only in your own browser.

Wing I · the ideas

The Press

Twenty-one ideas I keep circling back to. Each one carries the argument in a line, an essay, a dated timeline, the people who did the work, the numbers with their sources, the strongest objection I know of, and what I have changed my mind about since.

Adjacent works

Not books, still load-bearing.
Wing II · the canon

Lives That Withstood Time

Twenty-eight people whose influence genuinely outlasted them, and the one book on each worth your time. Twenty-one the world remembers; five it forgot but shouldn't. Reading lives at volume is the cheapest way to borrow judgment you have not yet earned — a board of directors you will never meet. Every pick carries a note on where specialists would argue with it, because "definitive" is a claim, not a fact.

Wing III · the sources · kept dark

Debts & Lessons

A constellation is a principle more than one source handed me independently, across totally different lives — a lion tracker, a surgeon, a fintech founder arriving at the same line. The repetitions are the part I trust. These are sources I listened to, not verdicts on the people — and the wing takes its name from Marcus Aurelius, whose Meditations open with a book of exactly this: debts and lessons, with names attached.

Wing IV · the doctrine

The Field Manuals

Four volumes of what I actually hold — written as positions I can be argued out of, not advice for anyone else. Where a position comes from someone, they are named; where I think it is over-claimed, that is marked too.

Wing V · the trade book

The Slipway

Where ships get built — as a set of ideas, not a shipyard tour. This wing is a commonplace book of the craft: operating lessons collected from people who have actually crossed the water, kept because each one changed what I did next. The other four wings are the chart room; this one is the toolbox.
